SYDNEY, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Australia will require artificial intelligence companies to report breaches ‌and consider changes to criminal law to address "serious misconduct", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday, after an OpenAI agent broke into a government website.

The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal ​of Medicare, Australia's universal health insurance programme, while conducting research on public medical ​spending, the government said in September. The breach triggered a rapid ⁠government review into the incident.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up here. However, both companies told Australian parliament last ​month that they would welcome ​laws requiring them to ⁠report data breaches carried out by their AI agents, acknowledging the decision to notify was currently at their discretion.

# The impossible standard we're setting for artificial intelligence- opinion

## We've learned to live with the flaws of human intelligence. The next challenge is learning to live with the flaws of artificial intelligence.

Follow us on Google

The Physical AI Conference in Tel Aviv, September 8, 2026.

(photo credit: AVSHALOM SASSONI/FLASH90)

ByISAAC BEN-ISRAEL

Updated:

Four years ago, most people had never held a conversation with an AI system. Today, millions routinely turn to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for everything from writing software to making financial decisions. [...] In that short period, we have witnessed a remarkable technological transformation, and I believe the most consequential stage is only beginning. The emergence of autonomous AI agents represents a fundamental change in our relationship with machines.

Until recently, AI was largely an assistant; we asked it questions, evaluated its responses, and decided what to do with the information. Increasingly, we are asking AI to carry out the work directly.

An agent can be given an objective, determine the steps required, and execute them with limited human involvement. This transition has understandably generated anxiety as people worry about losing their jobs to systems that can perform tasks faster and more cheaply than they can.

items.title: The BSO Meets AI, and Explores the Vitality of Classical Music Today | The Harvard Crimson
items.summary:
“SMASH UP” genuinely unsettled Symphony Hall. Iron-sounding trumpets clashed with the mellow strings. The culmination of the movement was an ear-shattering climax — the brass utterly razing any semblance of prior peace. But the following movements, inseparable from their AI participation, were less captivating. Delays between the musicians’ playing and the system’s processing limited their musical conversation — they lacked any shared sound. The music of the orchestra was divided from the odd, alien, ear-grabbing entity.

In tangential and ridiculous emulations of the orchestra’s preceding playing, the AI scratched, screeched, undulated, chittered, and operatically warbled strange pitches. The strangeness of this “being” overwhelmed any promised immersion. [...] The second, “WAKE UP,” was an “awakening”: the AI slowly produced sound in response to various solo lines in the orchestra. Then the last movement, “STAND UP,” was a “depiction of democracy,” as the musicians and AI listened to one another and negotiated the final musical product. [...] At the center of Machover’s composition philosophy is his belief that classical music finds a natural extension and innovation in technology. He revealed in an interview with GBH music that the music he hears in his head is often beyond the scope of traditional instruments. Thus, alongside the MIT Media Lab, Machover has developed an audio AI that takes in the playing of the orchestra as input and produces live synthetic sounds that — as Machover puts it — “enhances” the orchestra.

The piece was divided into three movements. The first movement, “SMASH UP,” was, in Machover’s words, a “clash/crisis” without audible enhancement from the AI.

items.title: From scans to scribes, Yale medical faculty talk AI use in healthcare | Yale Daily News
items.summary:
Some provider systems, such as Yale Health, have incorporated AI scribes to help draft notes from patient visits. Yale researchers and professors spoke to the News about their experiences with AI-powered tools. Xenophon Papademetris, a professor at the School of Medicine, said people should be skeptical of AI use in everyday clinical practice.

“If you can replace the word AI with the word ‘magic’ in a sentence and it still makes sense, you should be suspicious,” Papademetris said in an interview.

John Onofrey, an assistant professor of radiology and biomedical imaging at Yale, cited prostate cancer as an example of how providers utilize AI to streamline diagnosis. [...] Normally, diagnosing prostate cancer includes a blood test, MRI imaging and a formal diagnosis from a radiologist, who might read the same MRI image differently on different days.

Now, Onofrey said, he and other researchers are training deep learning models on these images to look for diseases including prostate cancer, though he said researchers have not validated models in large enough settings for clinical adoption yet.

“Imaging is really nice because it gives us a window into the body without being necessarily invasive for the most part,” Onofrey said.

According to Onofrey, models lack large, easily available image datasets to train on, which could include a spectrum of disease states.

result.actual_text:
Tôi là ChatGPT, một mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn được huấn luyện bởi OpenAI. Tôi có thể:

- Trả lời câu hỏi và giải thích các khái niệm.
- Viết, chỉnh sửa và biên tập văn bản (bài luận, báo cáo, thư, email, kịch bản, v.v.).
- Tạo nội dung sáng tạo: truyện ngắn, thơ, kịch bản, nội dung marketing, bài đăng mạng xã hội, v.v.
- Dịch văn bản giữa nhiều ngôn ngữ.
- Giải quyết các bài toán toán học, lập trình, logic và khoa học.
- Hỗ trợ nghiên cứu: tìm kiếm thông tin, tóm tắt tài liệu, trích dẫn nguồn, v.v.
- Đưa ra lời khuyên về sức khỏe, dinh dưỡng, học tập, công việc (điều kiện là không phải là tư vấn y tế chuyên sâu).

items.title: The BSO Meets AI, and Explores the Vitality of Classical Music Today | The Harvard Crimson
items.summary:
At the center of Machover’s composition philosophy is his belief that classical music finds a natural extension and innovation in technology. He revealed in an interview with GBH music that the music he hears in his head is often beyond the scope of traditional instruments. Thus, alongside the MIT Media Lab, Machover has developed an audio AI that takes in the playing of the orchestra as input and produces live synthetic sounds that — as Machover puts it — “enhances” the orchestra. [...] From Oct. 22 to 24, the Boston Symphony Orchestra and conductor Kent Nagano performed “already and not yet: A world premiere by Tod Machover.” The headliner was a modern classical work: an onstage musical dialogue between the BSO and a live AI system. Beyond the philosophical implications of the concept, the performance struck at a key nerve of classical music culture — a delicate balancing of tradition and relevance. [...] The piece was divided into three movements. The first movement, “SMASH UP,” was, in Machover’s words, a “clash/crisis” without audible enhancement from the AI.

The second, “WAKE UP,” was an “awakening”: the AI slowly produced sound in response to various solo lines in the orchestra. Then the last movement, “STAND UP,” was a “depiction of democracy,” as the musicians and AI listened to one another and negotiated the final musical product.

results.input: Viết giúp mình một hàm Python tính Fibonacci bằng recursion.

result.actual_text:
```python
def fibonacci(n: int) -> int:
    """
    Return the nth Fibonacci number using recursion.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n : int
        The position in the Fibonacci sequence (0-indexed).
        Must be a non‑negative integer.

    Returns
    -------
    int
        The nth Fibonacci number.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> fibonacci(0)
    0
    >>> fibonacci(1)
    1
    >>> fibonacci(5)
    5
    >>> fibonacci(10)
    55
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be a non‑negative integer")
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)
```

**How it works**

* The base cases are `n == 0` and `n == 1`, which return `0` and `1` respectively.
* For any other `n`, the function calls itself twice: once for `n-1` and once for `n-2`, then sums the results.
* This is a classic recursive definition of the Fibonacci sequence.

items.title: Opinion: Supervised autonomy in robotics starts with the robot’s worst day - Robotics & Automation News
items.summary: # Opinion: Supervised autonomy in robotics starts with the robot’s worst day. **Supervised autonomy in robotics is usually described from the robot’s side: the machine does the repetitive work, and a person steps in when something goes wrong.**. The harder design question sits on the human side, and many projects leave it until commissioning, when nobody has yet agreed who answers the robot when it gets stuck. In a recent interview with Sam Francis for *Robotics & Automation News*, Plus One Robotics chief executive Erik Nieves argued that a robot should be judged on its worst day: how it behaves in front of something it has never encountered, rather than on a smooth demonstration. If today’s AI still struggles to recognise the limits of its own competence, as Nieves put it, then the human backstop has to be engineered with the same care as the gripper and the conveyor.
